doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

title: Blindfold test: Cannonball Adderley
summary: Wilson identifies Cannonball and praises his tone, alto mastery, communication and Country Preacher.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: I’m going to play a couple of tunes, just little pieces for you. I guess we could call it a blindfold test. I’m sure that —

Yeah. Cannonball. I don’t know the particular recording, obviously one of the live recordings. I wanted to say — not “Mercy Mercy” but there’s a live recording called “I Know Why I Feel So Bad” something like that.
Yeah. “Why am I Treated So Bad.”

Yeah. Man Cannonball to me was the consummate altoist. His tone, his sound, his approach. And you look at his career, you could apply that tone to jazz, R&B, classical. When you listen to some of those records he did in the 50s with strings, the things —

“Fiddler on the Roof,” yeah. And there was another one like in the mid-50s, I can’t remember the title of it, I think he’s doing some Ellington pieces on there. And he’s playing in a very classical-like tone, but very expressive and very beautiful, it almost sounds like a cello sometimes. But he had to me just the consummate concept of alto saxophone, which for a lot of people who don’t know it’s like I always tell people it’s the easiest one to start on and the hardest one to master. The alto, playing it constantly has me in a headlock. It’s a really difficult instrument to master, and I’ve had this conversation with just every other altoist. You know John Gorton, who is a wonderful altoist, we talk about this a lot. I’ve had this conversation with Kenny Garrett and we always talk about yeah man that alto, ooh. But we keep at it. But for Cannonball, yeah, one of my favorites.
Yeah. He had such an electricity about him and his personality too. One of the few people who seemed comfortable talking with his audience and getting the music across from that standpoint.

Yeah and that’s very important. He was a great communicator both with and without the instrument. You listen to him talk, and he’s very eloquent, but very funny at times and right to the point. And you just — I got the chance to see him live when I think I was maybe twelve years old. And he just brings you right into the music. He brings you right in. And you listen to those records, like “Country Preacher” you know. I used to listen to that record for him talking as much as him playing.
His inflections and what he was saying.
You know that spot in the record where they’re doing “Country Preacher” and the first time it hits that break and there’s that silence? And when they come back in and the people go crazy.

Yeah it’s like church. Yeah. And that hit me directly. Because it was like going to church. So yeah Cannonball, to me represented the past, present and future. And he even mentions that on that record, when he talks about the past, present and future of our music.
And that’s really what it’s about.
